Compare two datasets the way PROC COMPARE does

Source: R/df_compare.R
df_compare.Rd

Each common variable belongs to a Type family: numeric (integer, double, logical), character (character, factor compared by labels), date or datetime (compared as instants, whatever the time zone). Variables of different families are Conflicting types and their values are not compared. The Comparison method and Criterion apply to the numeric family only; other families are compared exactly.

Usage

df_compare(
  base,
  compare,
  id = NULL,
  var = NULL,
  with = NULL,
  method = "exact",
  criterion = 1e-05,
  relative_delta = 0,
  ignore_trailing_blanks = TRUE,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  max_print = 50
)

Arguments

base

The Base dataset: the reference the comparison reports against. A data frame (including tibbles), an arrow Table or Dataset, or a duckdb table (a dbplyr lazy table on a duckdb connection).

compare

The Compare dataset, checked against base. Any of the types accepted for base, in any combination with it.

id

Character vector of ID variables used to pair observations, or NULL (the default) to match observations by position, as SAS does without an ID statement: the first Base observation with the first Compare observation, and so on. The extra observations of the longer dataset are then Unmatched observations, and differences() and unmatched_rows() identify observations by an obs column holding the observation number. Matching by position needs in-memory data frames, since the observation order of arrow and duckdb data is not guaranteed; for those, id is required.

var

Character vector of Base variables whose values are compared, as SAS's VAR statement; NULL (the default) compares every common variable. Each must be in both datasets, unless with names its Compare variable. var and with must not name ID variables, whose values are equal in every Matched observation by construction. See the Variable pairing section.

with

Character vector of Compare variables, as SAS's WITH statement: the same length as var, each paired by position with the var variable it is compared with. Results report the Base name.

method

The Comparison method for numeric variables: "exact", "absolute", "relative" or "percent", as SAS's METHOD=.

criterion

The Criterion the method tests differences against, as SAS's CRITERION=.

relative_delta

The constant δ that method = "relative" adds to the denominator, as in SAS's METHOD=RELATIVE(δ): a number between 0 and 1, 0 by default as in SAS.

ignore_trailing_blanks

If TRUE (the default), character values that differ only in trailing blanks are equal, as in SAS. Leading blanks always count.

ignore_case

If FALSE (the default), variable names are matched exactly, so USUBJID and usubjid are different variables. If TRUE, names that differ only in case are paired; see the Variable pairing section.

max_print

The most Unequal values the Listing shows per variable, as SAS's MAXPRINT=; the Listing notes when a variable has more. differences() always returns all of them.

Value

A df_compare object.

Details

Two missing values are equal and NaN counts as missing. Special missings (haven's tagged NAs, SAS's .A to .Z) are equal only with the same letter; this rule needs in-memory data frames, since arrow and duckdb do not keep the tags.

Variable pairing

A Base variable is paired with the Compare variable of the same name. Names are case-sensitive by default, unlike in SAS, so that a and A are never silently treated as one variable. With ignore_case = TRUE, names that differ only in case are paired instead, and id, var and with may be written in either dataset's case; results and the Listing always use the Base names. It is an error when two names in one dataset differ only in case, since the pairing would then be ambiguous.

As with SAS's VAR statement, var restricts only the comparison of values: Unequal values are reported for the var variables alone, while the Variables Summary (variables in only one dataset, Conflicting types, Attribute differences) still covers every variable, and so does the Return code. A Base variable paired by with is not a variable in only one dataset, and neither is its Compare variable; its Attribute differences are reported under the Base name.

Backends

The comparison runs as dplyr verbs inside the datasets' own backend; only observation counts and Unequal values are collected into R, never the full datasets. When the two datasets live in different backends they are brought into one without collecting them:

  • a data frame compared with a duckdb table is registered in the duckdb connection as a view;

  • a data frame compared with arrow data is converted to an arrow Table;

  • arrow data compared with a duckdb table is registered in the duckdb connection through arrow's zero-copy interface.

Two duckdb tables must share one connection. arrow, duckdb, dbplyr and DBI are optional; an informative error names any that an input needs but that is not installed.

Special missings that a backend does not preserve (for example haven tagged NAs in a duckdb table) are treated as absent for that dataset; for attributes, see the Attribute differences section.

Attribute differences

As PROC COMPARE does, df_compare() compares metadata as well as values. For each common variable and each with pair, ID variables included, the label, format.sas and width attributes (as set by haven when reading SAS files) are compared, and so is the data frame's own label attribute (the dataset label). An attribute present on only one side is an Attribute difference; one absent on both sides is ignored. Attribute differences are shown in the Listing's Variables Summary (dataset labels in its Dataset Summary) and set Return code bits 1 (dataset label), 8 (format), 16 (width) and 32 (variable label). They are never Unequal values: they don't appear in differences() and never set bit 4096.

Attributes are R metadata, so they are only as complete as the backend keeps them. Data frames (including tibbles read with haven) keep them. Arrow data keeps the R attributes it was created with, stored in its metadata; arrow data written outside R has none, so it is treated as having no attributes. Lazy database tables, such as duckdb tables, carry no R attributes at all: when either dataset is one, no attributes are compared and no Attribute differences are reported, rather than reporting false ones.
